content.problem: A candidate looks good on an average dashboard, yet performs badly for a small group of requests. Train and reload a tiny local artifact, compute predictions against a fixed evaluation set, then make the release decision from per-example and count-weighted slice metrics.
content.idea: A release pipeline connects data contracts, evaluation and artifact selection. This offline experiment serializes model parameters, reloads them as a consumer would, and derives every error from observed predictions and targets. Aggregate metrics summarize behavior, while required slices carry explicit gates and counts.
objectives: Evaluate predictions from a reloaded local artifact
Keep group-safe splits and count-weighted slice metrics
Separate code CI from model delivery
Interpret distribution change without inventing labels

sections.title: A passing average can hide a failing slice
sections.body:
Start with \(10\) held-out requests: \(9\) low-input rows and \(1\) high-input row. For candidate A, each low row has squared error \(0.01\), while the one high row has squared error \(4\). The low errors contribute \(9 \times 0.01 = 0.09\); adding \(4\) and dividing by \(10\) gives overall MSE \(0.409\). That average looks under the illustrative \(0.5\) limit, but the high-input row still fails its required slice gate. The decision needs both the aggregate and the slice policy.

The plot compares those same rows after reloading candidate A and candidate B. Counts tell you what each mean summarizes: \(9\) low examples, \(1\) high example, \(10\) overall. A count of \(1\) is a useful warning about how little evidence the high-slice mean represents. Monitoring later asks a different question: whether the input mix changed.

check.prompt: Why define a slice gate before inspecting candidate results?
check.answer: It makes the selection rule explicit and reduces post-hoc cherry-picking. The gate should reflect the application's requirements, with sample counts and uncertainty considered.

sections.title: Validate data before the expensive job
sections.body: Before training, inspect each row as a record with an ID, source group, split, numeric inputs and target, and declared slice. The fixture checks that the fields are known, numbers are finite, split and slice names are allowed, IDs are unique, and every source group stays in one split. A new row ID does not prevent leakage: if two rows came from the same subject but one is in train and one is in test, the model can indirectly see the held-out source during training. Reject that manifest before spending time on a job. Hashing the accepted rows gives later stages a way to identify which data was checked. In a feature pipeline, record event time, transformation version and missing-value rules so a changed serving input can be traced.

sections.title: Use a fixed release evaluation
sections.body:
The consumer reads candidate A back from its serialized file, predicts each held-out row, and squares prediction minus target. For low row low-0, prediction \(1.0\) against target \(1.1\) gives \((1.0 - 1.1)^2 = 0.01\). The \(9\) low rows each have that error, so their mean is \(0.01\). For high-0, prediction \(17.0\) against target \(19.0\) gives \(4.0\); because it is the only high row, its slice MSE is \(4.0\). The overall mean is the count-weighted sum, \(\frac{9 \times 0.01 + 1 \times 4.0}{10} = 0.409\).

Candidate B is separately saved and reloaded. Its high-slice offset changes the prediction for high-0 to \(18.9\), making that row's squared error \(0.01\). On the same \(10\) IDs, labels and policy, all three means are \(0.01\) and all gates pass. This comparison changes the candidate while keeping the evaluation fixed; the later label-correction check asks a different question.

sections.title: Separate code CI from model delivery
sections.body: Treat code CI and model delivery as connected stages with different evidence. Code CI checks the pipeline source, schema handling and numerical behavior. Model delivery then identifies a candidate, evaluates it on a frozen versioned set, packages the serving artifact and checks that package before promotion. A passing code test cannot certify a particular model's slice metrics, and a passing model evaluation cannot show that the next code change is safe. The example workflow isolates its MLflow SQLite store per job and its container step does not publish an image. A team should retain run metadata and artifacts outside temporary workers, and promote a recorded model/image pair only after both kinds of checks pass.

sections.title: Compare distributions without inventing labels
sections.body: Here the two-bin input mix moves from \(90\%\) low and \(10\%\) high to \(50\%\) low and \(50\%\) high. Total variation is half the sum of the bin changes: \(\frac{1}{2}(\lvert 0.9 - 0.5\rvert + \lvert 0.1 - 0.5\rvert) = 0.4\). This describes a substantial change under these declared bins; it says nothing directly about correctness because no new outcome labels are part of this calculation. First ask whether the change reflects a broken feature pipeline or a legitimate population shift. Keep distribution counts alongside delayed-label slice outcomes and service measures such as latency, so the next action follows the evidence available.

sections.title: Plan a response instead of a reflex
sections.body: Give the alert a named owner, a time window and a runbook step. If the high-input share rises, check schema and preprocessing first, then identify which requests changed and whether labels have arrived. A malformed-input spike may call for quarantine; a valid new population calls for collecting outcomes and comparing a candidate on an appropriate evaluation set. Consider rollback only if serving evidence or a valid comparison supports it. Retraining on corrupted inputs can encode the problem into a new model. Record sample counts with the alert because a short, small window can make an ordinary fluctuation look decisive.

sections.title: Rehearse the failed gate
sections.body: Walk the release evidence in order. The manifest validator accepts the separated groups, then the consumer reloads two distinct artifacts and evaluates the same \(10\) held-out IDs. Candidate A records low MSE \(0.01\) (\(9\) rows), high MSE \(4.0\) (\(1\) row), and overall MSE \(0.409\) (\(10\) rows), so its overall gate passes but the combined policy fails. Candidate B records \(0.01\) for all three groups and passes. The label-correction check holds A fixed and changes the high target from \(19.0\) to \(17.1\); its high error then becomes \(0.01\). That is evidence that evaluation labels matter, not evidence that A changed. A cross-split source group is rejected, and a run with no high-slice examples fails with count \(0\) and MSE unavailable. When reading a release report, check which input changed, the denominator for each mean, and whether every required slice is present.

commands.label: Run the standalone local MLOps experiment
commands.code: Save the lesson experiment as mlops_release.py and run: python mlops_release.py
commands.expected: Reloads the local model artifact and prints per-example predictions, slice gates and fixed-manifest comparisons.

content.output: Computed after reloading two distinct local artifacts. Candidate A: low MSE 0.01 (9), high MSE 4.0 (1), overall 0.409 (10), gate fails. Candidate B changes one high-slice offset parameter; on the exact same held-out IDs, targets, splits, slice counts and 0.5 policy it has low MSE 0.01, high MSE 0.01, overall 0.01 and passes. A separate fixed-artifact label-correction check is reported separately.
content.exercise: Compare the two reloaded artifacts at the same ten held-out IDs and fixed policy. Change only candidate B’s high-slice offset from 1.9 to 0.5, then report its per-example high-slice error and gate result. Distinguish that candidate comparison from the separate label-correction sensitivity check.
content.solution:
# This separate check changes one candidate parameter while freezing the labels.
changed_b=dict(artifact,slice_offsets={'high':.5})
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as work:
    path=Path(work)/'changed-b.json'; path.write_text(json.dumps(changed_b))
    per_c,metrics_c,_=evaluate_reloaded(rows,path,.5)
assert [(v['id'],v['target'],v['slice']) for v in per_c]==[(v['id'],v['target'],v['slice']) for v in per]
assert math.isclose(metrics_c['high']['mse'],2.25,abs_tol=1e-12)
assert not metrics_c['passed']
high_example=next(v for v in per_c if v['slice']=='high')
assert math.isclose(high_example['squared_error'],2.25,abs_tol=1e-12)
print('candidate B high-slice example:',high_example)
print('candidate B with offset 0.5:',metrics_c)
print('Artifact A and B are distinct:',digest(artifact)!=digest(changed_b))

experiments.title: Tighten one shared release policy without changing either model
experiments.prediction: Candidate A has high-slice MSE \(4\), while B has MSE \(0.01\). With the same ten cases and a shared limit of \(0.005\), should either model pass? Compare that decision with the original \(0.5\) limit.
experiments.code:
# Change only the shared policy; preserve both serialized artifacts and evaluation rows.
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(prefix='mlops-policy-change-') as folder:
    policy_root=Path(folder)
    policy_results={}
    for name,saved_model in [('A',artifact),('B',candidate_b)]:
        model_path=policy_root/(name+'.json')
        model_path.write_text(json.dumps(saved_model,sort_keys=True))
        fixed_cases,strict_metrics,_=evaluate_reloaded(rows,model_path,.005)
        _,original_metrics,_=evaluate_reloaded(rows,model_path,.5)
        assert [(r['id'],r['target'],r['slice']) for r in fixed_cases]==[(r['id'],r['target'],r['slice']) for r in per]
        assert strict_metrics['overall']['count']==original_metrics['overall']['count']==10
        assert strict_metrics['low']==original_metrics['low']
        assert strict_metrics['high']==original_metrics['high']
        assert not strict_metrics['passed']
        policy_results[name]={'original_pass':original_metrics['passed'],'strict_pass':strict_metrics['passed']}
    assert policy_results=={'A':{'original_pass':False,'strict_pass':False},'B':{'original_pass':True,'strict_pass':False}}
print('Same predictions, changed policy:',policy_results)
experiments.output: At the original limit, A fails and B passes. At the stricter shared limit, both fail, although neither model prediction nor case identity changed.
experiments.explanation: A release decision depends on a declared policy as well as observed errors. Tightening the threshold must not change the underlying metric values. Both candidates here are predefined synthetic teaching artifacts; the offset is not a claim of a learned improvement on an independent real task.

practice.title: Change the population mix
practice.prompt: Keep each slice’s measured error fixed, but evaluate nine high-slice examples and one low-slice example. Recompute the weighted overall MSE from errors produced by the reloaded artifact.
practice.hint: Change counts rather than the model errors.
practice.solution:
# `metrics` was computed from per-example errors after loading the local artifact.
low_mse=metrics['low']['mse']; high_mse=metrics['high']['mse']
new_low_count=1; new_high_count=9
weighted=(new_low_count*low_mse+new_high_count*high_mse)/(new_low_count+new_high_count)
assert math.isclose(weighted,3.601)
assert low_mse==metrics['low']['mse'] and high_mse==metrics['high']['mse']
print('new weighted MSE:',weighted,'unchanged slice MSEs:',low_mse,high_mse)
practice.explanation: Aggregate performance changes with population mix even when each slice’s error is unchanged. Report both before attributing the change to a model regression.

content.question: An input drift alert fired before new labels arrived. What follows?
options: Retrain and automatically replace the active model.
Investigate the change and gather quality evidence before choosing a response.
Declare accuracy has decreased by the drift score.
content.explanation: An unlabeled drift alert is evidence of a distribution change under the detector, not direct evidence of accuracy loss. Investigate data integrity, affected slices, service health and delayed outcomes. Retraining and promotion require their own declared quality gates.
content.diagnosis: Check denominators and slice counts before thresholds. A missing slice, nonfinite metric or changed evaluation manifest should block comparison. Investigate drift and training-serving skew separately from service health.
takeaways: Validate data before the expensive job

visual.title: An average can conceal the failing slice
visual.prediction: Which bar would an aggregate-only dashboard hide?
visual.reading: On the same \(10\) held-out rows, candidate A has overall MSE \(0.409\), low-slice MSE \(0.01\) across \(9\) rows, and high-slice MSE \(4.0\) on \(1\) row. Candidate B has MSE \(0.01\) in all three groups. The dashed \(0.5\) line is the illustrative limit: A's overall bar sits below it, but its high-slice bar exceeds it; B clears every gate. The denominator printed in each label tells you how many rows support that bar.
visual.connection: Each bar is calculated from squared prediction errors after the named artifact is reloaded. The paired run holds case IDs, targets, splits, slice counts and the \(0.5\) policy fixed while changing candidate B's high-slice offset. The separate label-correction check holds candidate A fixed and changes one target, so it is not a third candidate comparison.
visual.alt: Candidate A has overall MSE 0.409 and high-slice MSE 4; candidate B has overall and high-slice MSE 0.01 under the same ten examples and threshold 0.5.
